Issued at 159 PM MDT Wed Oct 21 2026

HAZARDOUS WEATHER POSSIBLE THROUGH FRIDAY: 

Remnant moisture from a tropical cyclone formerly known as 
Trudy is moving northeastward across eastern Utah and western 
Colorado. A plethora of weather hazards are possible with this 
system including flooding, flash flooding, strong to severe 
thunderstorms, and snow above 12,000-13,000 feet. As a result, a
Flood watch is in effect for parts of southeast Utah and 
southwest Colorado through 12 PM Friday. 

This afternoon:

An initial push of convection has developed over the Four 
Corners region and will pose a localized threat for heavy 
rainfall and flash flooding if stronger storms develop, 
especially if storms begin to train over the same areas. 
Isolated severe storms capable of producing large hail, damaging
wind, and brief tornadoes cannot be ruled out due to the 
presence of modest instability and strong shear. However, the 
highest potential for severe weather will remain off to our 
southwest strong downstream blocking ridge will favor the 
trough over the West to linger upstream of us through early 
Tuesday. This will keep us in strong Southwest flow aloft and a 
generally warmer and moist environment. As mentioned earlier the
highly anomalous tropical plume will be advecting north of the 
area tonight but still remain above normal until the trough 
passes and we begin to dry out after midweek. Winds will remain 
breezy in the leading edge of the trough with gusts of 25 to 35 
mph...with a few higher gusts possible in the 4 Corners region 
tomorrow afternoon. Higher gust over the terrain can be expected
as well. The parent low in this trough is over the Oregon this 
evening and model consensus has it digging through the 
Intermountain West to the 4 Corners region by Tuesday evening. 
This will keep broad ascent over our area supported by the jet 
aloft which will keep working on the moisture to produce showers
through Tuesday morning. The best chances will be over the 
western 2/3 of the CWA and the San Juans with less coverage over
the central divide. Ascent increases significantly through the 
day Tuesday as the upper low digs through the lower Great Basin.
This will ooze a cold front through the area under the strong 
QG signal in northwest into central Arizona. Stay weather aware
if you have outdoor activities planned! If you experience any 
of the hazards noted above, please report them to NWS Grand 
Junction.

Tonight - Thursday night: 

With an anomalously moist tropical airmass overhead, widespread
rainfall takes hold of the forecast area Wednesday night. 
Please see the Hydrology Section below for more information 
concerning the threat for flooding from this period of moderate 
to widespread rainfall. 

Another round of strong to severe storms cannot be ruled out on
Thursday afternoon/evening with marginal instability and strong
wind shear present. However, widespread cloud cover adds a 
layer of uncertainty to the forecast and may inhibit surface 
heating. If stronger storms develop, isolated damaging wind, 
large hail, brief tornadoes are possible. We have low confidence
in this aspect of the forecast. 

Friday: 

Models have continued to key in on a dry slot quickly 
evacuating the tropical moisture from the region on Friday 
morning. Even after it stops raining, the risk for flooding will
remain elevated on Friday morning as water continues to work 
through the system. Do not let your guard down right away! We'll
have a better idea of how long flooding may continue to cause 
issues after we get a better sense of how much rainfall is 
received on Thursday. 


LOOKING AHEAD:

Chances for light precipitation (valley rain, mountain snow 
above 10,000 feet) continue through the weekend as a low 
pressure system, currently spinning off the California coast, 
traverses the Intermountain West. Plenty of uncertainty remains 
in how this low will evolve as it moves inland, but ensemble 
guidance tends to show a weakening system by the time it reaches
our forecast area. Regardless, this system will provide enough 
forcing for scattered to widespread precipitation as it moves 
through, alongside a brief reduction in temperatures.
